blocks.title: Right now you have {{three bad options}}
blocks.description: Every cleaning operator picks one of these, and all three cost money. None of them is a failure of effort.

cards.title: Answer it yourself, between jobs
cards.description: You take the call in the van or mid-clean. You quote from memory, you write the address on your hand, and you lose the thread when the next call comes. Spam and price-shoppers cost you the same interruption as a real lead.

cards.title: Let it go to voicemail and call back later
cards.description: Most people never leave a message. The ones who do have already called two competitors by the time you finish the job, and getting hold of them again takes three attempts across two days.

cards.title: Pay an answering service to take a message
cards.description: You are billed per call or per minute, so your busy season is your most expensive month. They cannot see your calendar or your rates, so the job still is not booked — it just arrives as a message for someone to action.

blocks.infoNote: None of the three books the job. That is the part worth fixing.

blocks.title: What your AI receptionist {{actually runs}}
blocks.description: The whole intake-to-rebook lifecycle of a cleaning business — including the three parts nobody else automates.

cards.title: Answers Every Call
cards.description: First ring, any hour, including the stacked mornings when every crew is already on site and the office is empty.

cards.title: Texts Back Missed Calls
cards.description: Anything that still slips through gets a text in seconds, while the prospect is on your listing and not the next one.

cards.title: Scopes the Job
cards.description: Beds, baths, square footage, pets, access codes and add-ons captured in conversation rather than a form people abandon.

cards.title: Quotes From Your Rates
cards.description: Applies your flat rates, minimums and service-area rules — and refuses to quote the jobs you said need a walk-through.

cards.title: Books the Crew
cards.description: Holds a real slot against crew availability and writes the job into the scheduling tool your office already works from.

cards.title: Confirms and Reschedules
cards.description: Sends confirmations, arrival windows and reminders, and moves an appointment when the customer asks — without a call to you.

cards.title: Sells the Recurring Plan
cards.description: Offers weekly, biweekly or monthly service at the moment the one-time clean is booked, which is the only moment it reliably lands.

cards.title: Backfills Cancellations
cards.description: A 7 a.m. cancellation is a crew with a paid-for empty morning. The agent works your waitlist and recent quotes to fill the slot instead of leaving it stranded.

cards.title: Chases Quotes and Follows Up After the Visit
cards.description: Unconverted estimates get worked on your schedule, and after the clean it checks satisfaction, asks for the review when it went well, and hands the conversation to a person when it did not.

blocks.note: Recurring plans, cancellation backfill and post-visit follow-up are where cleaning margin actually lives — and where every other AI receptionist stops.

blocks.title: What the silence {{actually costs}}
blocks.description: Most calculators price a missed call as one job. In this business a recovered caller is usually a recurring contract, which is a different number entirely. Move the sliders to your own week.
blocks.clientsLabel: new clients a month you are not booking
blocks.annualLabel: over a year, if they stay
blocks.frequencyLabel: How often a new client books
blocks.breakEvenNote: One recovered client covers the platform for months. The sliders start deliberately low, because the argument only works if you can check it.
blocks.assumptionNote: What this assumes: the annual figure holds only if those clients stay the year, and it ignores referrals and reviews. What it leaves out entirely: cancellations you could have backfilled, and quotes that went cold without follow-up. It is an estimate you can argue with, not a promise.

blocks.title: The questions operators actually ask about

items.question: What happens if it quotes the wrong price on a job that turns out to be a disaster?
items.answer: You decide what it is allowed to price. Standard sizes and services quote from your rate card; anything you flag — hoarding, post-construction, biohazard, unusual square footage, commercial — it will not put a number on. For those it collects the details, says the price needs a look first, and books the walk-through instead. You can also cap it to a range rather than a fixed figure.

items.question: Does it work for our service mix — one-time deep cleans, recurring maid plans, commercial janitorial?
items.answer: Yes, and it treats them differently. One-time jobs are scoped and priced on the spot, with the recurring plan offered at the point of booking. Recurring customers are recognised, so it handles schedule changes and renewals instead of re-qualifying them. Commercial and specialty work follows its own path, including routing to a walk-through.

items.question: Can it fill a slot when someone cancels at 7 a.m.?
items.answer: That is one of the jobs it is worth pointing at first. When a cancellation lands it can work your waitlist and your recent unconverted quotes to offer the freed slot, so a crew that is already paid for does not sit idle. You set who gets offered what, and whether it may discount.

items.question: How does it avoid double-booking a crew or sending them across town?
items.answer: It books against real availability in your scheduling tool rather than a separate calendar, so it can only offer slots that exist. Service-area and travel rules are yours to define — by zone, by postcode, or by how much drive time you will accept between jobs — and it declines or escalates anything outside them.

items.question: What does the agent handle alone, and when does a person step in?
items.answer: It handles standard intake end to end: qualifying, quoting, booking, confirming, reminding, rescheduling and following up. You decide what it never decides alone — non-standard pricing, complaints, damage claims, contract terms — and it hands those over with the full conversation attached rather than starting the customer again.

items.question: Will our customers know they are talking to AI?
items.answer: That is your call. It can introduce itself as an assistant, or simply answer as your business. Either way it does not pretend to be a specific named employee, and it hands off rather than bluffing when a caller asks something outside what you gave it.

items.question: Who owns the customer data and the call recordings?
items.answer: You do. Conversations, recordings and records stay in your account and are never used to train public AI models. You set retention windows and can export or delete the data whenever you want.

items.question: Can it take a deposit or keep a card on file?
items.answer: It can collect payment details through your existing processor as part of the booking, so deposits and cancellation terms are enforceable rather than aspirational. Card data goes to the processor, not into the conversation record.

items.question: Does it handle Spanish-speaking customers?
items.answer: Yes — it answers in the language the customer uses and keeps one thread, so a caller who switches between Spanish and English mid-conversation is not starting over. Worth configuring deliberately if a meaningful share of your customers or crews prefer Spanish.

items.question: How long does deployment take?
items.answer: Typically a few days to a couple of weeks. What moves that number is how ready your inputs are: a clear rate card, service-area rules, access to your scheduler and CRM, and the escalation rules you want. Starting from a template and letting the AI Concierge draft the canvas removes most of the setup.

items.question: What happens when it gets something wrong?
items.answer: It will, occasionally — any intake process does, including a human one. Every conversation is logged with a timestamp, so a mis-scoped job is traceable rather than mysterious, and you tighten the rule that allowed it. Set the escalation threshold conservatively at launch and loosen it once you have seen a few hundred real conversations.

items.question: How do credits map to call and message volume?
items.answer: Credits are consumed by what the agent runs — conversation turns, channel usage and the actions it takes in your systems — so a quiet week costs less than a busy one. There is no monthly fee and no per-seat charge, and credits do not expire. Current per-channel rates and packages are on the pricing page.

items.question: Can we use the platform beyond the front desk later?
items.answer: Yes. The same canvas runs recruiting intake for cleaners, dispatch and crew messaging, collections reminders and reporting workflows. Most operators start with inbound booking because it pays for itself first, then reuse the same connections for the next process.
